blocks.text: The cell cycle has four separate phases: **G1** (growth phase 1), S (the synthetic phase), **G2** (growth phase 2) and M (mitosis phase).

Cells in the quiescent **G0** phase are stimulated by growth factors (**EGF**, **PDGF**, **IGF**), which activate transcription factors and start **DNA** synthesis, followed by mitosis and cell division. From **G0** the cell moves to **G1**, when the chromosomes are prepared for replication.

blocks.text: Cell division distributes replicated genetic material from a parent cell equally to two daughter cells. Before mitosis the cell undergoes interphase, the 'holding' stage between two consecutive divisions, in which genetic material and organelles are replicated; it is the longest phase and all cell-cycle steps (**G0**, **G1**, **G2** and S) except M make up interphase.

blocks.text: Human cells are diploid: 46 chromosomes, 23 from each parent, forming 23 homologous pairs (22 pairs of autosomes plus two sex chromosomes). X and Y are not homologous: males are **XY**, females **XX**. Gametes are haploid because meiosis halves the chromosome number.
Chromosomes are classified by size and shape (largest = chromosome 1). The centromere divides each into a short p arm and a long q arm.

blocks.text: Cells with a chromosome number different from the normal diploid are aneuploid, e.g. trisomy 21, trisomy 18 or the monosomy of Turner's. Rarely a whole extra set is present: triploid (69 chromosomes) or tetraploid (four sets); triploidy and tetraploidy result in spontaneous abortion.

Aneuploidy arises from non-disjunction (failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate) in meiosis: one gamete gets two copies and another none, giving a trisomic or monosomic fetus. Only individuals with trisomy 13, 18 and 21 survive to birth, and most children with trisomy 13 and trisomy 18 die in early childhood.

Non-disjunction in mitosis soon after the two gametes fuse gives two cell lineages with different chromosomal make-up (a 'mosaic'). This is more frequent with the sex chromosomes, and mosaics show milder malformations than complete aneuploidies.

Chimerism versus mosaicism: two or more cell lines from **DIFFERENT** zygotes in one individual is chimerism; in mosaicism the distinct cell lineages all originate from the **SAME** zygote (the explanation's contrast).

blocks.text: In Turner's syndrome, in ==80%== of cases the origin of the aneuploidy is the paternal X chromosome; hence the single X present is of maternal origin. Random X inactivation does not occur in cells with a single X chromosome.

Turner's **IQ** profile (notes): girls show a disharmonic **IQ** profile. Full-scale **IQ** is comparable to the general population or lower by a mean of 10 points (nearly one **SD**), mostly from reduced performance **IQ** (at least 20 points / 1 **SD** lower), with verbal **IQ** preserved. Visuospatial subtests (Block Design, Object Assembly) may be affected more; mathematical ability may be lower. The profile persists into adulthood.

Females with a 45X karyotype may have higher verbal skills if the single X is paternally derived instead of maternal (maternal is most common), suggesting an imprinted gene that is inactive when carried on a maternally derived X chromosome.

blocks.text: Genetic information is stored as double-stranded **DNA**. **DNA** and **RNA** are nucleic acids made of nucleotides; nucleotides are phosphorylated nucleosides, and each nucleoside has two components: a nitrogenous base and a pentose sugar.
The pairing that does **NOT** occur in human **DNA** is **TG** (A pairs only with T, C only with G).
The two **DNA** strands twist into a double helix. **RNA** is single stranded in human cells.

blocks.text: A gene is a sub-portion of **DNA** coding for a polypeptide sequence. A set of three adjacent nucleotides is a codon, coding for a specific amino acid. There are 20 amino acids but 64 possible codons, so most amino acids are encoded by more than one triplet; other codons signal initiating or terminating polypeptide-chain synthesis.

The notes state humans have 3 x 109 bp (as printed) of total chromosomal **DNA** of which protein-coding genes constitute only 32 000 bp (as printed).

blocks.text: Transcribed **RNA** initially contains non-coding introns and is called heterogeneous nuclear **RNA** (hnRNA). hnRNA undergoes splicing (the notes say aided by nucleosomes in the nucleus) to remove the non-coding sequences, giving messenger **RNA** (mRNA). tRNAs are synthesised from **DNA** in the nucleus in a separate process.

Amino acid activation: tRNAs entering the cytoplasm are attached to specific amino acids in an energy-dependent process catalysed by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase in the presence of Mg2+; there is a separate enzyme for each kind of amino acid. The energy in activated amino acids is used to make peptide bonds.

Translation has three steps - initiation, elongation and termination. The ribosome has a peptidyl (P) site where methionine-containing tRNA initially binds and an aminoacyl (A) site where each new incoming tRNA with its activated amino acid binds. Chain termination is signalled by one of the codons **UAA**, **UGA** or **UAG**.

The Golgi complex is a dynamic system acting as a temporary protein repository that gives off vesicles and vacuoles for processing and transport. Modifications include covalent modification, protein folding and tagging with signal peptides. Recognised posttranslational modifications: glycosylation, proteolysis, phosphorylation, gamma carboxylation, prenylation, ubiquitation, polyamination and nitration. The process also tags wrongly folded or aberrant proteins for destruction in lysosomes.
Study of mRNAs using microchip arrays is called transcriptomics.

blocks.caption: Flowchart (page 7): DNA Sequences -> EXONS (coding) and INTRONS (non-coding); INTRONS -> Tandem Repeats and Interspersed. Minisatellite -> Telomeric repeats (necessary for integrity of chromosomes) and Hypervariable repeats (used in DNA fingerprinting). Interspersed -> Long Interspersed Nuclear Elements and Short Interspersed Nuclear Elements.

blocks.text: A mutation is a sudden, permanent and heritable change in the **DNA** sequence; it is transcribed to mRNA and can be translated into protein, leading to disease expression.

blocks.title: Classification of mutations
rows: Single-base alteration, usually a substitution (one base replaced by another)
Purine replaced by another purine, or pyrimidine by another pyrimidine (e.g. A to G)
Purine replaced by a pyrimidine or vice versa (e.g. A to T)
Deletion or insertion not in multiples of three (e.g. 5-base deletion); shifts the reading frame with variable results
Changes in multiples of 3 bases; no disturbance of the reading frame
No change in protein product (one amino acid is often coded by more than one triplet)
New codon specifies a different amino acid, variable effect; e.g. haemophilia, sickle cell anaemia
New codon signals 'stop', giving a non-functional protein (printed as '**UUA** **UGA** or **UAG**')

blocks.text: Point substitutions do not shift the reading frame; they often occur in non-coding regions and go unnoticed, and even in coding regions they are often silent or mis-sense.
Translocation is exchange of chunks of genetic material between chromosomes ('larger' mutations). Most are reciprocal (one segment exchanged for another).

Robertsonian translocation is non-reciprocal and fuses two acrocentric (non-homologous) chromosomes into a single metacentric fusion chromosome; the small p arms are discarded with only trivial loss of genetic material, so the carrier is viable and 'balanced'.

In gamete formation only one gamete can have the whole fusion chromosome, so a fertilised gamete without it is monosomic (unbalanced) and the gamete with it is trisomic. This is one mechanism for Down's syndrome, and with a carrier mother the recurrence rate of Down's is extremely high compared with sporadic Down's from non-disjunction.

The form of Down syndrome as likely to come from the father as from the mother is the Robertsonian translocation (not mosaicism, duplication, deletion or full trisomy 21): two acrocentric chromosomes break at their centromeres and the long arms fuse, with the short arms lost after a few cell divisions.

blocks.text: Mendel (a Catholic priest working with garden peas) proposed the laws of inheritance. First law, uniformity: crossing plants differing in one trait gives hybrids uniform in that trait. The notes add this is not entirely true, as later geneticists showed intermediate phenotypes from co-dominant heterozygous expression.
Second law, the principle of segregation: for any trait the pair of alleles of each parent separate and only one allele passes from each parent to the offspring; which one is a matter of pure chance.

Third law, independent assortment: different pairs of alleles are passed to offspring independently, so new combinations present in neither parent are possible (blue eyes do not take brown hair 'with it'). The notes add that segregation was later proved true by studying chromosomes during cell division.

Mendelian traits are categorical (all or none); not applicable in the same simple way to IQ or blood pressure.

blocks.text: Autosomal dominant: one mutated copy is enough because the normal gene product cannot compensate, so a heterozygote manifests the disease. Offspring of heterozygotes have a ==50%== chance of inheriting the disease allele and so the disease; if both parents are heterozygous the recurrence risk is ==75%==.

Incomplete penetrance: a patient has a dominant disorder that does not manifest clinically, giving the appearance of a skipped generation, and increasing the likelihood of an unaffected child. Variable expression: differences in severity (a mildly affected parent may have a severely affected child).

Spontaneous disease-causing mutations often present as diseases known to be autosomal dominant: achondroplasia and tuberous sclerosis are commonly spontaneous mutations although families show an **AD** pattern. The abnormal gene in autosomal dominant disease often codes for structural proteins such as receptors or cytoskeleton proteins.

Phenocopy (Goldschedt, 1935): a phenotypically indistinguishable disorder without the genotype, e.g. antipsychotic medication causing the same symptoms as genetically determined Parkinson's disease; also genotypically determined Pendred syndrome being mimicked by endemic cretinism.

Autosomal recessive: manifests only when homozygous for the disease allele. Parents are generally unaffected carriers (heterozygous), there is usually no family history although the gene can pass (skip) through generations, and the offspring of an affected person are healthy heterozygotes unless the other parent is also a carrier. Consanguinity increases the risk, and the abnormal gene often codes for enzymatic proteins.

X inactivation: a mechanism (random, very early in female embryos) that compensates for the Y chromosome's small genetic contribution. The inactivated X is seen as a highly condensed Barr body in interphase nuclei and is not transcribed. It is random (some cells inactivate the paternal X, others the maternal), irreversible and fixed for life, and the cell's progeny keep the same inactivation. All X chromosomes in a cell are inactivated except one, so trisomy X females have two Barr bodies. X inactivation occurs via **DNA** methylation.

X-linked recessive: a single recessive mutation on a man's only X causes disease; a female needs a double identical mutation (extremely rare). If most normal-allele X chromosomes are inactivated by chance (unfavourable Lyonisation), females become manifesting heterozygotes, usually with mild disease that can go unnoticed. Skipped generations are common because an affected male can pass the mutation to a phenotypically normal heterozygous daughter who transmits it to her sons.
Male-to-male transmission is not seen in X-linked inheritance. Examples of X-linked recessive disease given: haemophilia A/B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and androgen insensitivity syndrome.

X-linked dominant disorders are rare; males transmit to all daughters and no sons, and females are twice as likely as males to inherit the mutation. Vitamin D-resistant rickets is the best-known example, and Rett's syndrome (an atypical pervasive developmental disorder) is inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion. The phenotype is seen in multiple generations, so skipped generations are relatively unusual.

Hyperuricaemia with developmental delay, dystonia and **IQ** 60 in a child = Lesch-Nyhan, with self-injurious behaviour.
Noonan syndrome is the autosomal dominant disorder among Friedreich ataxia, **PKU**, Hurler and Tay-Sachs (explanation: 1:1000-1:2000, short stature ==80%==, cardiac abnormalities >==80%==).
A 3-year-old girl with intellectual disability and stereotyped hand movements around the midline = Rett syndrome, X-linked dominant (almost exclusively females).
Sex-linked recessive: all daughters of an affected father are carriers (phenotypically normal, transmit to their sons); females need two identical mutations for disease expression.
Autosomal recessive transmission: risk is high with consanguinity ('hidden relatives' carry the gene) - not pure maternal transmission, not male-to-male, not sex-limited.
==25%== of children affected although both parents are apparently healthy = autosomal recessive (the less common the allele, the likelier the parents of a homozygote are consanguineous).

X-linked dominant: rare; Rett syndrome and vitamin D-resistant rickets; affected father gives all daughters, no sons.

blocks.text: Mitochondrial inheritance, mosaicism, trinucleotide expansions and genomic imprinting do not follow Mendelian principles (non-Mendelian inheritance). Polygenic and multifactorial disorders also do not strictly obey Mendelian principles.

Mitochondrial **DNA** is wholly inherited from the ovum: the sperm head has no mitochondria, and the body and tail (which hold the mitochondria) are shed on entry, so embryo mitochondria are completely maternal. The mitochondrial chromosome has no introns in its genes, so any mutation has a high chance of having an effect. Most mitochondrial diseases are myopathies and neuropathies.

Mitochondrial **DNA** codes for 13 proteins of the respiratory chain plus 22 tRNAs and 2 ribosomal RNAs. Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (**LHON**) is the commonest cause of blindness in young men (bilateral loss of central vision, cardiac arrhythmias) and is purely maternally inherited.

blocks.title: Mitochondrial disorders named in the notes
rows: Mitochondrial myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and recurrent stroke syndrome (also 'stroke-like episodes')
Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy: bilateral central vision loss and cardiac arrhythmias; commonest cause of blindness in young men
Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres (an encephalomyopathy)
Ophthalmoplegia, heart block, cerebellar ataxia, deafness and mental deficiency due to long deletions and rearrangements

blocks.text: Trinucleotide repeat disorders are caused by trinucleotide repeats (e.g. **CGG**, **CTG**, **CAG**) in certain genes exceeding the normal number of repeats; the mutation gives an unstable, often fragile, site.

Anticipation: in the most recent generations of an affected family the disease appears at an earlier age and with greater severity than in previous generations, mostly due to gradual expansion of trinucleotide repeats (this instability is a 'dynamic mutation').
Anticipation = earlier onset and more severity with successive generations; the 'least likely' statement is that onset age and severity **REDUCE**.

blocks.caption: Four boxed headings (page 14): Frag(g)ile X syndrome - cGG; Friedreich AtaxiA - gAA; Huntington ChoreA - CAg; MyoTonic dysTrophy - cTg.

blocks.title: Trinucleotide repeat disorders (source figure and text)
rows: Expansion proximal to **FMR1**; anticipation higher in maternal transmission
Anticipation higher if the expansion comes from the mother

blocks.mnemonic: The source figure writes the disease names with some letters capitalised next to the repeat: Frag(g)ile X - cGG; Friedreich AtaxiA - gAA; Huntington ChoreA - CAg; MyoTonic dysTrophy - cTg.

blocks.text: Fragile X: accounts for more cases of mental retardation in males than any condition except Down syndrome, with a frequency of ==1 in 4000==; females are affected ==50%== less often than males. It results from expansion of a **CGG** repeat proximal to the **FMR1** gene; if the repeats increase beyond 52 the sequence destabilises and can expand further during spermatogenesis or oogenesis.

blocks.title: Fragile X: repeat number and consequences (as stated)
rows: Destabilises the sequence, allowing further expansion during spermatogenesis or oogenesis
Women premutation carriers: increased risk of premature ovarian failure and/or mild cognitive or behavioural abnormalities
Increased repeats without full phenotype; increased risk of intention tremor and ataxia, especially after middle age
Lower **IQ** in most men and ~==60%== of women

blocks.text: Fragile X, 'most likely' statement: intelligence is correlated with the load of chromosomal damage (**CGG** repeats at q27, with macrocephaly and mental retardation in childhood); the distractors are a q25 deletion, microcephaly, adolescent-only onset and **CTG** repeats.

Clinical features: affected males have enlarged testes, prominent ear lobes and a protracting jaw, a high-pitched voice and mental retardation. Heterozygous women, with a compensating second X, show no physical signs other than early menopause, mild learning difficulties and rarely frank retardation.

Learning disability with expressive language disorder, social anxiety, impulsivity and marked inattention points to fragile X syndrome - molecular testing shows an expansion of **CGG** repeats (Xq27.3), not **CAG**, **CTG**, **CCCG** or **GCC**.
Fragile sites: **FRAXA** at the first exon of **FMR1**; **FRAXE** at Xq28 is also linked to mental retardation; **FRAXF** is the third folate-sensitive fragile site but is not linked to **MR**.

Huntington's disease: autosomal dominant with full penetrance, prevalence about 5 per 100,000. An expanded unstable **CAG** repeat on 4p16.3 gives an extended glutamine sequence in huntingtin (expressed throughout the body, function unclear). Onset is usually between 30 and 50 years. Most adult-onset cases have 40-55 **CAG** repeats, while more than 70 repeats are seen in childhood-onset **HD**. Characteristic protein deposits form nuclear inclusions in neurons.

Anticipation in **HD** is greater when the disease comes from the father (greater repeat expansion and earlier onset); nearly one-third of father-to-offspring cases show an expansion giving juvenile-onset **HD**.
Huntington's **NOT** true statement: 'maternal inheritance results in more severe and earlier onset' - the explanation is that spermatogenesis induces more instability in **HD** (paternal expansion).

Myotonic dystrophy (**CTG** repeat expansion): anticipation is higher when the expansion is inherited from the mother, because oogenesis, with its long dormancy compared with spermatogenesis, gives much higher instability. The notes also say Fragile X anticipation is higher by maternal than paternal inheritance, in contrast to Huntington's.

blocks.title: Parent-of-origin effect on anticipation
rows: Maternal inheritance (oogenesis gives much higher instability)
Paternal inheritance (greater repeat expansion, earlier onset)

blocks.text: Anticipation in **PATERNAL** transmission: Huntington's disease is the keyed condition (not Noonan, Hurler, Lesch-Nyhan or tuberous sclerosis); the explanation defines anticipation as earlier onset or greater severity in recent generations, mostly from gradual trinucleotide repeat expansion (dynamic mutation).

Genomic imprinting: no structural differences between maternally and paternally inherited chromosomes, but there are subtle functional ones. A paternally inherited 15q11-q13 deletion gives Prader-Willi syndrome (**PWS**); a maternally inherited deletion of the same region gives Angelman's syndrome (**AS**). The maternal 15q11-13 is expressed in the brain and hypothalamus (neuronal damage in its absence). Imprinting is thought to be due to **DNA** methylation, and is a parent-of-origin exception to Mendelian patterns.

blocks.title: Prader-Willi vs Angelman syndrome
rows: Maternal **UPD** in most of the remaining (==25%==)
Obesity, short stature, small limbs, decreased **IQ** with hyperphagia and skin picking
Developmental delay, low **IQ**, jerky movements especially hand-flapping, frequent smiling, seizures

blocks.text: Prader-Willi syndrome, correct statement: associated with short stature (explanation: often short statured and obese with learning disabilities); the distractors are 'occurs only in males', social anxiety as a common feature, normal **IQ** and a life expectancy of 6 to 8 years.

Multifactorial inheritance: multiple genes together with environmental influences. Common psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia are not Mendelian; they are defined as present or absent but treated as quasi-continuous (the affected can be graded by severity). The liability/threshold model assumes an underlying liability, continuously (normally) distributed, with those past a threshold manifesting the condition; relatives of affected individuals have a liability distribution shifted to the right.

Recurrence risks to relatives in multifactorial disorders are influenced by disease severity, degree of relationship to the index case, number of affected close relatives and, if one sex has a higher incidence, the sex of the index case.

blocks.title: Multifactorial vs polygenic inheritance
rows: Most common psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia
Height and intelligence (normally distributed continuous characteristics)

items.text: Maternal transmission only, no paternal transmission, affecting both sexes = mitochondrial inheritance (mtDNA from the ovum only; 37 genes in the explanation).
In Fragile X premutation carriers: increased risk of intention tremor and ataxia (not 'no clinical features').
Deletion of **PATERNALLY** derived 15q11-q13 = Prader-Willi (maternal = Angelman).
Abnormal trinucleotide expansions are detected by **PCR**.
Social anxiety and gaze avoidance among trinucleotide expansion syndromes = fragile X syndrome (eye-gaze avoidance is a striking feature).
Recurrence risk higher in a family with three affected children than one with two = multifactorial inheritance; Mendelian recurrence risks are unaffected by the number of offspring already affected.

Huntington's 'least likely' statement: normal gene has 35-45 **CAG** repeats - explanation: normal is about 7-28 triplets, 29-35 will not develop **HD** but may pass an expanded allele, 40 or more develop **HD**.
Huntington's disease: **IT-15** gene ('interesting transcript 15') on chromosome 4, with an unstable expanded trinucleotide repeat - not presenilin-1 (chr 14) or **APO** **E4** (chr 19).

bullets.text: Mitochondrial DNA is purely maternal (no sperm mitochondria); no introns so mutations bite; MELAS, LHON, CPEO, MERRF, Kearns-Sayre type disorders.
Trinucleotide repeats: Fragile X CGG, Friedreich GAA, Huntington CAG, myotonic dystrophy CTG; anticipation = earlier/worse with each generation.
Fragile X: 1 in 4000, CGG beyond 52 destabilises, 200+ repeats lower IQ; premutation carriers get tremor/ataxia (women: ovarian failure).
Huntington's: AD, full penetrance, CAG on 4p16.3, 40-55 repeats adult onset (30-50 y), >70 juvenile; paternal expansion.
Myotonic dystrophy and Fragile X: anticipation higher maternally (oogenesis); Huntington's higher paternally.
Imprinting: paternal 15q11-q13 deletion = Prader-Willi (~70%, maternal UPD ~25%); maternal deletion = Angelman (paternal UPD ~4%).
Multifactorial = genes + environment (liability/threshold); polygenic = additive genes, no environment.

blocks.text: A polymorphism is variation in genetic make-up at a locus in the general, apparently healthy population. To qualify, the variant must occur in at least ==1%== of the total population and be associated with normal but varied (not disease-causing) phenotype expression; spontaneous mutations are excluded because they cannot occur in that proportion. **ABO** blood groups are the example.

blocks.title: Types of polymorphism
rows: Variation that changes the sites at which restriction enzymes cut **DNA** (Southern blotting)
Change in a single nucleotide; assayed by **DNA** sequencing or **DNA** chips
Length polymorphism / **VNTR** (variable number of tandem repeats)
Varying numbers of repeats in a specific region
2 to 6 bases; currently preferred genetic markers for disease mapping because they can be detected with **PCR**

blocks.text: Polymorphisms arise from mutations but are maintained by founder effect, genetic drift and natural selection. Most occur in non-coding areas (introns), since mutations in exons often produce disease.

Statement true of polymorphisms: maintained by evolutionary processes (the explanation: must occur in at least ==1%== of the population; evolutionary selection is assumed to maintain them) - **NOT** 'above ==6%==', not functional defect, not exon-only.

Serotonin transporter polymorphism (5HTTLPR, in the non-coding promoter region) has a short and a long variant (length polymorphism); ==55%== of Europeans carry the long allele. The short variant has low serotonin transporter expression and is speculated to be linked to affective disorders, neuroticism, anxiety and **PTSD**, but the evidence is inconclusive (mostly case-control studies with heterogeneity).

Caspi et al. (2003): individuals with one or two copies of the short allele of the 5-**HTT** promoter polymorphism showed more depressive symptoms, diagnosable depression and suicidality in relation to stressful life events than those homozygous for the long allele (gene-environment interaction).

items.text: Genetic variation across the population without overt phenotypic change = polymorphism (not mutation).
Southern blot visualises restriction fragment length polymorphisms.

blocks.subtopic: SLC6A4 and chromosomal position of the serotonin transporter
blocks.note: **Q84** answer **SLC6A4**: the explanation says 5HTT is encoded by **SLC6A4** (solute carrier family 6, member 4) on chromosome 17q11.2, and that the S allele lowers transcriptional efficiency, serotonin transporter binding and uptake. The notes discuss 5HTTLPR (short/long, ==55%== of Europeans long) but never name **SLC6A4** or give its locus.

bullets.text: Polymorphism = variant in at least 1% of the population with normal (non-disease) phenotype; ABO blood groups.
RFLP (Southern blotting), SNPs (sequencing/DNA chips), VNTRs: microsatellites 2-6 bases (preferred, PCR), minisatellites 20-70 bases.
Maintained by founder effect, genetic drift, natural selection; mostly in non-coding regions.
5HTTLPR is in the promoter; short allele = low transporter expression; 55% of Europeans have the long allele.
Caspi 2003: short-allele carriers show more depression/suicidality after stressful life events (gene-environment interaction).

blocks.title: Blotting techniques
rows: Named after Dr E. M. Southern, who introduced it in 1975
Sample run on polyacrylamide gel, blotted to a membrane, membrane incubated with antibody to the protein

blocks.forTopic: Which blot detects what (Southern, Northern, Western)
blocks.mnemonic: SNOW DROP: Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = Protein

blocks.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansions are **DNA** abnormalities, so Southern blot is the keyed detection method (not Northern blot, **ELISA** or Western blot; **PCR** is among the options but is not the key here).

Polymerase chain reaction (**PCR**) amplifies minute amounts of **DNA** (buccal scrapings, blood spots, single embryonic cells) over a million times in vitro, between two short single-stranded oligonucleotide primers complementary to the ends of the target; the exact **DNA** sequence to be amplified must be known. It is not error free, as laboratory contaminant **DNA** can be amplified.

blocks.title: The three steps of PCR
rows: Double-stranded **DNA** is denatured by heat into single strands; cooling favours annealing and the primers bind their targets
**DNA** polymerase extends the primers in opposite directions using the target **DNA** as template; one cycle gives two double-stranded copies, two cycles four, rising exponentially
The cycling is set to give the necessary number of amplifications

blocks.text: **NOT** a **PCR** step: vector-based replication of **DNA** (that is cloning); also **NOT** a **PCR** step: gel electrophoresis.

**FISH** (fluorescent in situ hybridisation) detects and localises specific **DNA** sequences on chromosomes using fluorescent probes that bind only parts of the chromosome with a high degree of sequence similarity, seen by fluorescence microscopy.

**DNA** cloning: a plasmid (extra-chromosomal, independently replicating bacterial **DNA**) can receive a **DNA** fragment of interest via **DNA** ligase; plasmids so used are called vectors (bacteriophages and other viruses can also be vectors). Replication of the vectors gives multiple copies (clones) of the inserted sequence, which can then be removed to give large quantities of the gene.

items.text: The best technique for detecting a large sequence of **DNA**: Southern blotting (it locates a particular **DNA** sequence within a complex mixture); **FISH** locates a sequence on a given chromosome.
Vectors go with **DNA** cloning (not **PCR**, **FISH** or Western blotting); a vector provides a backbone for the insert to be reproduced in bacteria.
Abnormal trinucleotide expansions are detected with **PCR** (relatively simple **PCR**-based assays); karyotyping shows large missing/extra material, **FISH** shows known sequences.

**NOT** a step in **PCR**: gel electrophoresis (the steps are denaturing the **DNA** by heat, annealing the primers on cooling, and extending the primers with **DNA** polymerase over repeated cycles).

blocks.note: **Q34**: the investigation of choice for Klinefelter's syndrome is karyotyping (explanation: white blood cells cultured and checked for an extra X; prenatal diagnosis by **CVS** or amniocentesis). The notes' cytogenetic techniques section covers blotting, **PCR**, **FISH** and cloning only, not karyotyping.

**Q14**: culturing cells under thymidine deprivation aids diagnosis of fragile X syndrome (explanation: it makes the fragile sites of the chromosome obvious for detection). The notes name fragile sites but not this detection method.

**Q43**: the best test for diagnosing Huntington's disease is **PCR** (explanation: serum **PCR** counts trinucleotide repeats - more than 35 in adults and more than 50 in children; the gene is at 4p16.3; a karyotype reveals only macroscopic defects such as deletions, translocations or trisomies). Not in the notes' **PCR** section.

bullets.text: Southern = DNA, Western = protein, Northern = RNA.
PCR: primers needed, so target sequence must be known; amplifies over a million-fold from tiny samples; contaminants can be amplified.
PCR has three steps: heat denaturation, cooling/annealing with primers, polymerase extension; cycles double the copies.
FISH uses fluorescent probes to localise specific DNA sequences on chromosomes.
DNA cloning inserts a fragment into a vector (plasmid, bacteriophage or virus) using DNA ligase to make clones.
Thymidine-deprived cell culture makes fragile sites visible for diagnosing fragile X.
Huntington's disease is diagnosed by PCR repeat counting (more than 35 repeats in adults, more than 50 in children); karyotype shows only macroscopic defects.

blocks.text: A twin pair is concordant when both co-twins have the same disease expression (or both are disease free) and discordant if only one has the disease. If a disease has a significant genetic component, concordance should be higher in monozygotes than dizygotes; a trait with no genetic basis should have equivalent **MZ** and **DZ** concordance.

Heritability is the main measure of genetic variation in polygenic (quantitative) traits: the proportion of total variation in a population that is genetic rather than environmental. Narrow-sense heritability = proportion of total phenotypic variance due to additive genetic variance; broad-sense heritability = proportion explained by total genetic variance (additive and non-additive). Non-additive influences include epistasis (gene-gene interaction) and dominance effects. Heritability can be calculated from concordance rates.

blocks.caption: Table (page 19), "Interpretation of heritability" (Visscher et al., 2008): columns STATEMENT / ACCURACY; six statements each marked CORRECT or FALSE with an explanation.

blocks.title: Interpretation of heritability (Visscher et al., 2008)
rows: A high heritability means most of the variation observed in the present population is caused by variation in genotypes
**CORRECT** - in the current population the phenotype of an individual is a good predictor of genotype
A heritability of ==80%== means ==80%== of the variability in whether an individual becomes affected is inherited, ==20%== is not
**CORRECT** - but it does not mean genes account for ==80%== of the causative factors (inheritance is not the same as genetic causation)
**FALSE** - environment can change or be manipulated to alter the phenotype
Heritability is the proportion of a phenotype passed on to the next generation
**FALSE** - only the genotype is passed on; many modifiers lie between genotype and phenotype
Heritability is informative about the nature of between-group differences
**FALSE** - it is measured within a specified population; group differences may not be genetic
A large heritability implies genes of large effect
**FALSE** - not true for polygenic disorders; no strong relation between heritability and number/size of genes. Exception: Mendelian single-gene disorders all have heritability of ==100%==

blocks.text: Obesity (regarded as environmental) shows high familial loading: ==80%== of offspring with both parents obese, ==40%== with one parent obese, versus ==10%== with both parents lean. Heritability estimates for **IQ** from twin studies are consistent at 0.5-0.8.

blocks.caption: Table (pages 19-20): columns Disorder / Heritability estimate*; rows Schizophrenia 80, Bipolar disorder >80, Major depression 40, Generalized anxiety 30, Panic disorder 40, Phobia 35, Alcohol dependence 60 (the table continues from page 19 onto page 20).

blocks.title: Heritability estimates by disorder (approximations, DSM-IIR based)

blocks.text: Autism and Tourette's may have around ==90%== heritability (Owen, Cardno and O'Donovan, 2000).

Notes vs question bank on bipolar heritability: the notes give bipolar heritability as >80 (disorder table, p19-20) and 'broad heritability nearly 85-==90%==' (genetics of mood disorders, p31). **Q57** (answer 75-==85%==) gives 0.75 to 0.80 in its explanation. If asked in the exam, pick the option that fits 75-==85%== when offered; know that the notes quote higher figures.

items.text: Heritability is a measure of the genetic contribution to phenotypic variation in a population (not of an individual's disease, nor of penetrance or **MZ** concordance).
==75%== heritability = ==75%== of the liability for the disease is inherited (not ==75%== of patients, or ==75%== risk in first-degree relatives).
Of the options **IQ**, neuroticism, extraversion, bipolar disorder, novelty seeking, bipolar disorder has the highest heritability.
Twins alike for hair colour but different for iris colour: they are concordant for hair colour; a trait with no genetic basis would have equal **MZ** and **DZ** concordance.

bullets.text: Concordance: MZ > DZ implies a genetic component; equal MZ and DZ concordance implies none.
Heritability = proportion of trait variance that is genetic; narrow-sense (additive) vs broad-sense (additive + non-additive).
High heritability does NOT mean genetic determination or genes of large effect; Mendelian single-gene disorders = 100%.
Heritability estimates: schizophrenia 80, bipolar >80, major depression 40, GAD 30, panic 40, phobia 35, alcohol dependence 60.
Autism and Tourette's may be about 90% heritable; IQ 0.5-0.8; Big Five 42-57%.

sections.title: 11. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, epistasis, heterogeneity and pleiotropy

blocks.text: In the absence of mutation, non-random mating, selection and genetic drift, the genetic constitution of a population stays the same from one generation to the next.

Worked example in the notes: disease incidence ==1 in 3600== live births, so q squared = 1/3600 and q = 1/60; p = 1 - q = 59/60; carrier frequency 2pq = 1/30, i.e. ==1 in 30== of the whole population are heterozygous carriers.

blocks.caption: Shaded text box (page 20), "Genotype frequency": definition of genotype frequency and gene frequency with the worked example of 100 individuals (33 AA, 45 AB, 22 BB).

blocks.text: Genotype frequency = count of each genotype divided by the total number of individuals (example: 33 **AA**, 45 **AB**, 22 **BB** in 100 gives 0.33, 0.45, 0.22). Gene frequency is the proportion of chromosomes in a population carrying a specific allele; the notes work it as 2 x 33 + 45 = ==111%== or 1.11 for allele A and 2 x 22 + 45 = ==89%== or 0.89 for B (figures as printed).

Notes vs question bank on gene frequency: the notes' worked example prints allele-frequency figures of 1.11 and 0.89 (which sum to 2). **Q21** (**HH** 50, hh 10, Hh 40; answer 0.7) divides the allele count by the 200 gene copies in 100 people: H = 50 + 50 + 40 = 140; 140/200 = 0.7. Use the divide-by-2N method from the question; do not copy the notes' un-divided figures.

Carrier frequency shortcut (**Q37**): for an autosomal recessive disorder in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with incidence ==1 in 4900==, the carrier frequency is twice the square root of the disease frequency, giving ==1 in 35== (explanation: carrier frequency is twice the square root of the frequency of the disease). Compare the notes' ==1 in 3600== example giving ==1 in 30==.

blocks.title: Why Hardy-Weinberg does not always hold
rows: Genes that hinder survival and fertility are not maintained; some mutations with survival benefit are kept at higher than expected rates (sickle cell carriers protected against severe falciparum malaria; cystic fibrosis carriers may have an advantage against typhoid)
Gene frequency change from limited population size; explains why some genetic diseases are unusually common in small isolated populations; very close to the 'founder effect'
Exchange of genes between populations (migration etc.), so populations are not 'closed'
Non-random mating; mutations preserved within a closed pedigree; autosomal recessive diseases more often seen in consanguineous families
Environmental exposure can provoke more mutations than expected (e.g. living near a nuclear reactor leak)

blocks.text: Schizophrenia genes kept at a low level because affected people marry less and have fewer children = natural selection (not assortative mating, genetic drift, pleiotropy or negative eugenics); the explanation cites impaired fertility and onset at reproductive age.

blocks.caption: Shaded text box (page 21), "Epistasis, heterogeneity & pleiotropy": definitions of epistasis, locus heterogeneity, allelic heterogeneity and pleiotropy with the printed examples.

blocks.title: Epistasis, heterogeneity and pleiotropy
rows: Gene-gene interaction, particularly between different alleles at different genes; can occur at the same step or different stages of a biochemical pathway
Same disease phenotype caused by mutations at different loci; matters when testing specific loci
Same disease phenotype from different mutations at the same locus
Cystic fibrosis: nearly 600 different mutations at the same site on chromosome 7
A single disease-causing mutation affects multiple organ systems; common in genetic diseases
Marfan's syndrome: cardiovascular, connective tissue, skeletal systems

blocks.text: Two parents **BOTH** affected by the same autosomal recessive disorder have a clinically normal child = locus heterogeneity (not incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, pleiotropy or allelic heterogeneity): each parent may carry a mutation at a different locus, so the child is a heterozygous carrier at both (explanation example: presenilin 1, 2 and beta-**APP** mutations all causing similar presenile Alzheimer's).

items.text: Same phenotype from mutations at different loci = locus heterogeneity (not allelic heterogeneity, epistasis or pleiotropy).
One genetic alteration influencing another so that they mitigate each other = epistasis.

blocks.note: **Q72**: a person with schizophrenia more likely to marry someone with a psychiatric problem or substance use = assortative mating (explanation: preference for sexual partners with similar phenotypes). The notes' list of reasons Hardy-Weinberg fails (selection, drift, gene flow, consanguinity, mutation rate) does not include assortative mating.

bullets.text: Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1; p squared normal homozygote, q squared affected, 2pq carriers.
Notes' example: incidence 1 in 3600 gives q = 1/60 and carriers 2pq = 1/30.
HWE fails with selection, genetic drift (founder effect), gene flow, consanguinity, and high mutation rates.
Locus heterogeneity = same phenotype, different loci (early onset AD: chromosomes 1, 14, 21).
Allelic heterogeneity = same locus, different mutations (cystic fibrosis, ~600 mutations on chromosome 7).
Pleiotropy = one mutation, many organ systems (Marfan's); epistasis = gene-gene interaction.
Two affected AR parents with a normal child = locus heterogeneity (different loci in each parent).

facts.label: CF mutations at same site (allelic heterogeneity)

blocks.text: Gene mapping is any strategy that finds the chromosomal location of one or more genes, often disease-related; it needs no knowledge of the gene's function. Not all genetic studies map genes: family, twin and adoption studies mainly show whether a genetic influence exists. Gene mapping studies are linkage analysis, sib-pair analysis and, to some extent, allelic association studies.

Twin studies: monozygotic (**MZ**) twins arise when one embryo cleaves early, giving genetically identical embryos (==70%== share the same chorion). Dizygotic (**DZ**) twins arise from two ova fertilised by two sperm and share ==50%== of their genes, like siblings.

Pairwise concordance = twin pairs in which both have the disorder / total pairs. Probandwise concordance = affected twins / total co-twins (where systematic ascertainment, e.g. a twin register); it is more useful because it allows comparison of general population risk with the rate in co-twins of probands.

blocks.text: Linkage analysis: during prophase I of meiosis homologous chromosomes exchange **DNA** (crossover/synapsis); a crossover between two loci can give a new combination of alleles (a recombination). Loci farther apart are more likely to recombine, so recombination measures distance. Alleles of close loci on the same chromosome (syntenic) are inherited together (linked); unlinked loci have a ==50%== chance of transmission, whereas linked loci recombine in less than ==50%==.

Recombination frequency (observed in families) measures genetic distance, expressed in centiMorgans (cM). One cM = ==1%== recombination frequency between two loci, and 1 cM is approximately 1 million base pairs (1 Mb). Crossovers are more common at telomeres and less common near centromeres.

The **LOD** score (log10 of the odds: probability of the observed recombination frequency / probability that the recombination frequency is ==50%==, i.e. chance) lets scores from different families be added. **LOD** >3 is usually taken as statistical evidence of linkage (linkage 1,000 times more likely than non-linkage); **LOD** of -2 or less is conventionally evidence of non-linkage (non-linkage 100 times more likely).

blocks.title: LOD score thresholds

blocks.text: Linkage disequilibrium: specific combinations of alleles at two loci are seen together on chromosomes more often than expected by chance; it is more likely for very closely linked loci (rare recombination) and can be analysed in association studies.

blocks.title: Two approaches in linkage studies

Genes are identified through their positions in the genome rather than their functions; supported by the human genome project

blocks.text: Linkage analysis needs a large number of highly polymorphic markers dispersed throughout the genome.

Sib pair analysis: several hundred evenly spaced **DNA** markers are genotyped in concordant sibling pairs. Siblings share 0, 1 or 2 alleles at a marker with probability 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25; increased sharing at a marker suggests it is linked to a susceptibility locus (successful for type 1 diabetes). Loci of very small effect (relative risk <2) may need 600 to 800 sib pairs; in schizophrenia the sibling relative risk is about 10, so if several additive genes act, none may individually exceed 2.

Whole genome scan: a type of linkage analysis typing markers at regular intervals across the genome; tedious but often the first approach when nothing is known about a phenotype. Example: Stefansson et al. typed 950 microsatellite markers in 110 Icelandic patients with reconstructed genealogies and found neuregulin-1 to be a candidate gene for schizophrenia.

Association studies are simpler than linkage studies: a case-control design compares allele frequencies at a marker locus. They cannot make strong causal inferences, and false positives occur if populations are not matched for ethnic background. Loci studied are 'candidate genes'. Parents or relatives can provide controls (non-transmitted alleles) - the Transmission Disequilibrium Test (**TDT**). Genome Wide Association Studies (**GWAS**) do not use the candidate gene approach: thousands of SNPs are assayed in thousands of individuals.

sections.title: 12C. Alternative approaches: transgenics, epigenetics, position effects, endophenotypes

blocks.text: Transgenic studies: transgenesis is the transfer of a gene from one species to another; in practice often insertion of a modified mouse gene into the mouse genome to study gene function - a direct and powerful approach.

Epigenetics (term coined by Waddington): a second, equally complex layer of information from modifications beyond the **DNA** sequence. **DNA** methylation and histone modification explain most of the epigenetic variation found so far. Crow argued that epigenetic defects explain most of the concordance seen in schizophrenia (hemispheric laterality and language specialisation unique to human brains being the source of the defect).
Position effects: gene activity can depend on the precise chromosomal location and its 'neighbourhood', so genes show altered activity after translocation even if the gene itself is not disrupted.

Endophenotypes (Gottesman and Shields, 1975): unseen but measurable phenomena in the pathway from distal genotype to disease; they can be biochemical, neuroimaging, electrophysiological, pathological, neuropsychological or socio-functional markers.

blocks.title: Gottesman's criteria for an endophenotype (read from the PDF, p27)
rows: Must be associated with a candidate gene or region
Must be present with a high relative risk in relatives, thus cosegregating with actual illness
Must be a parameter associated with disease with biological plausibility
Must be independently expressed in clinical state (a trait marker, not a state)
Must be present in relatives more often than the general population

blocks.text: Breaking a complex construct such as schizophrenia into endophenotypes should allow Mendelian-style study: the simpler the construct, the fewer genes on the causal pathway. Probable endophenotypes for schizophrenia: working memory defects, information processing defects such as prepulse inhibition, smooth pursuit defects, glial cell changes and other neurocognitive markers.

**NOT** a reliable endophenotype for schizophrenia: negative symptoms - the explanation says clinical symptom clusters do not fit the criteria (associated with illness in the population, heritable, state-independent, co-segregating in families, higher rate in unaffected relatives); working memory defects, prepulse inhibition, smooth pursuit defects and glial cell changes are acceptable.

A genotype is the sum total of the genes inherited by an organism; an endophenotype is an internal phenotype discoverable by a biochemical test or microscopic examination (Gottesman and Shields).

Chromosome 21 harbours mutant **APP**, which is related to Down's syndrome and explains the higher prevalence of **AD** in Down's syndrome.

rows: 3.2 times (up to 5 times in some studies)

blocks.text: ApoE4 and Alzheimer's: the question keys 'five fold' (explanation: a single **E4** allele gives up to a three- to fivefold increase in **AD** risk), while the notes' table gives 3.2 times for heterozygotes (up to 5 times in some studies) and 14.9 times for homozygotes - note both figures and the allele count in the stem.

ApoE4 '**EXCEPT**' question: **E4** is implicated in Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, susceptibility to herpes simplex virus infection, poor recovery from head injury, intracerebral haemorrhage and elective cardiac bypass surgery - but **NOT** sporadic **CJD** (the answer).

Notes vs question bank on ApoE4 risk: the notes give odds 3.2 (heterozygote) and 14.9 (homozygote) vs 3/3 homozygotes, with the absolute-risk table. **Q9**'s explanation instead says that of people with no **E4** about ==20%== develop **AD**, with one **E4** ==50%== (2-3x higher), and with two **E4** ==90%==; the answer key is 'Three times higher (**OR**=3)' for a heterozygote. Both sets of percentages are in the sources and they differ; know the **OR** of about 3 for **E4** heterozygotes.

Risk in relatives: predicted risk of **AD** in first-degree relatives of probands is 15-==19%== compared with ==5%== in controls (3-4 times, to age 85), i.e. between one in five and one in six. For probands who became demented late (80s), relatives probably run the same 30-==50%== risk as anyone living to 90+. Risk drops rapidly with genetic distance (second-degree relatives probably less than twice population levels). Probandwise concordance is about ==40%== for **DZ** and ==84%== for **MZ** twins.

blocks.caption: Shaded text box (page 34), "CADASIL": text on amyloid angiopathy, NOTCH3, exon 4 and the 96% mutation detection rate.

blocks.text: **CADASIL** (as the notes describe it): a form of amyloid angiopathy that can present with Alzheimer's-like features. **NOTCH3** is the only gene currently known to be associated (19p13.1-13.2); most mutations are in exon 4 and the mutation detection rate is up to ==96%== in well-defined or biopsy-proven **CADASIL**.

Notes vs question bank on **CADASIL**: the notes call **CADASIL** 'a form of amyloid angiopathy'; the **Q79** explanation expands it as cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy, an inherited subcortical small-vessel disease where a Notch3 mutation causes granular deposits in small artery walls, narrowing lumens and destroying smooth muscle. The shared exam fact is Notch3.

Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (**FTLD**) refers to three syndromes: frontotemporal dementia (**FTD**), progressive non-fluent aphasia and semantic dementia. Some patients show tau pathology; familial cases have mutations in **MAPT** (microtubule-associated protein tau) on 17q21. Many cases are tau-negative with ubiquitin-immunoreactive neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions; some of these have progranulin (**PGRN**) mutations, also on 17q21. Progranulin is a widely expressed growth factor with roles in wound repair and inflammation, and is linked to tumorigenesis.

Lewy body dementia: no specific genetic associations established; mutations at the alpha-synuclein locus are reported inconsistently. **DLB** is one of the 'synucleinopathies' (synuclein aggregating in presynaptic terminals to form Lewy bodies), along with Parkinson's disease and multisystem atrophy.

blocks.text: Alpha-synuclein is expressed throughout the brain and has potential roles in learning, synaptic plasticity, vesicle dynamics and dopamine synthesis.

items.text: Late-onset senile Alzheimer's = chromosome 19 ApoE; the others (chr 1 presenilin 2, chr 14 presenilin 1, chr 21 beta amyloid) are associated with the presenile, early-onset type.
A 55-year-old with gradual memory loss and **MMSE** 20/30: the implicated gene codes for presenilin-1 (chromosome 14, young-onset **AD**).

Mutation in the progranulin locus: primary progressive aphasia (**GRN** frontotemporal dementia spectrum: bvFTD, **PPA** - progressive non-fluent aphasia and semantic dementia - and movement disorders).
**CADASIL**: Notch3 gene (not dysbindin, **LRRK2**, Parkin or **COMT**).
Down syndrome and Alzheimer's: the implicated gene is the amyloid precursor protein (**APP**, chromosome 21) - not presenilin 1/2, tau or ApoE4.
Alzheimer's strongly associated with **APO** **E4** on chromosome 19 (not presenilin-1 on chr 1, presenilin-2 on chr 2, **COMT** on chr 21 or **CAG** repeats on chr 4).
48-year-old with dementia: presenilin - the commonest cause of early-onset (<65 years) dementia is Alzheimer's via presenilin 1, presenilin 2 or amyloid precursor protein mutations.
53-year-old with gradual memory loss and **MMSE** 17/30: **PSEN-1** - **PSEN1** mutations are the commonest cause of early-onset **AD** (up to ==70%== of cases).

bullets.text: Familial early-onset AD: APP (chr 21), presenilin 1 (chr 14), presenilin 2 (chr 1); up to 50% of familial presenile AD but <1% of all patients.
APOE (19q): highest attributable risk; 4/4 OR 14.9, 3/4 OR 3.2; onset two decades earlier in 4 homozygotes.
ApoE absolute risk: 4 homozygote 35% male / 53% female; 4 heterozygote 12% / 23%; no 4: 4.6% / 9.3%.
First-degree relatives of AD probands: 15-19% vs 5% in controls (3-4x); MZ 84% vs DZ 40% probandwise concordance.
CADASIL: NOTCH3 on 19p13.1-13.2; mutations mostly exon 4.
FTLD: MAPT (tau) and progranulin (PGRN) both on 17q21.
Lewy body dementia: no specific gene; Parkinson's loci PARK1/4 (alpha-synuclein 4q21), PARK2 (Parkin 6q25), PARK8 (LRRK2), PARK6 (PINK1), PARK7 (DJ-1).

facts.label: AD risk, first-degree relatives vs controls

blocks.text: Autism: recurrence in siblings of autistic children is ==2%== to ==8%== (relative risk 50 times, range 30-120); the risk in a sibling of two autistic children is 25-==30%== (nearly 300 times higher).

Autism twin studies: ==60%== concordance for classic autism in **MZ** twins vs 0 in **DZ**; for a broader autistic phenotype ==92%== in **MZ** and ==10%== in **DZ** pairs, translating to ==90%== heritability. The identity and number of genes are unknown; chromosomes 2, 7 and 15 are implicated; segregation analysis was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance with sex-specific modifications.

Autism epidemiology: the true statement is heritability above ==90%== (explanation: **MZ** concordance ==60%== for classic autism vs 0 in **DZ**; ==92%== vs ==10%== for the broader phenotype, translating to ==90%== heritability) - the '**MZ** concordance above ==95%==' option is false.

Autism is associated with single-gene disorders: fragile X is the most clearly documented (perhaps ==8%== of autistic subjects have the cytogenetic fragile X; ==16%== of fragile X males are autistic); probable associations also with tuberous sclerosis, neurofibromatosis and phenylketonuria.

Phenotypic expression varies as much within **MZ** twins as between **MZ** pairs, suggesting non-genetic influences matter (LeCouteur, 1996). Risk for the broader phenotype (delayed speech, reading/spelling difficulties, social reticence, poor social language) in first-degree relatives and **DZ** twins is ==30%==; the spectrum phenotype has ==82%== concordance in **MZ** twins.

blocks.title: ADHD genetics
rows: Risks higher for male relatives, lower for female; unclear if higher when the proband is female

blocks.text: Personality disorders: the largest factor, nearly ==50%== or more of variation in most personality traits, is non-shared, person-specific environmental variation. Antisocial **PD** has the highest heritability (60-==70%==) among personality disorders; emotional dysregulation is highly heritable in borderline **PD**. A tryptophan hydroxylase gene variant is associated with low **CSF** 5-**HIAA** and suicide attempts in violent criminal offenders.

Personality disorder with the strongest genetic support: schizotypal disorder is keyed (explanation: familial risk is seen in schizotypal, antisocial, dependent and avoidant, but molecular and twin evidence most strongly implicate genetics for schizotypal); the notes separately give antisocial **PD** the highest heritability (60-==70%==) among personality disorders.

Panic disorder: lifetime prevalence about ==4.7%==; Hettema et al. (2001) family-study meta-analysis **OR** 5 in first-degree relatives (absolute risk 8-==31%==). Early-onset confers more risk: nearly 17-fold if onset before 20 vs 6-fold after 20. Heritability about 0.43.

Social phobia: 10-fold increase in first-degree relatives of probands with generalised social phobia; non-generalised discrete social phobia shows no familial transmission. Specific phobias are 3-4 times more common in first-degree relatives (**OR** 4), though twin data suggest individual-specific environment matters more.

Alcoholism: risk in families may be 4 to 6 times that of the general population. Most adoption studies show risk in adoptees correlates with biological rather than adoptive parents (3-4 times higher); no protective effect of being raised away from drinking biological parents (Goodwin 1973); risk is clearly higher in males, weak in females.

Alcohol genes: **GABRA2** variants (chromosome 4p) associated with alcohol dependence, strongly with impulse-control problems (risk allele also in adolescents with conduct disorder and drug-dependent alcoholics). **ADH** breaks alcohol into acetaldehyde, further metabolised by **ALDH**; both have variants linked to the flushing reaction, the strongest alcoholism finding being **ADH4** (early onset of regular drinking). A meta-analysis of 21 studies shows 50-==100%== increased alcoholism risk in carriers of the **DRD2** **A1** allele, though this may reflect a neighbouring gene.

**OCD**: early onset suggests higher genetic risk (generally onset before 18). Fathers were three times as likely as mothers to receive a diagnosis for probands with severe childhood **OCD**; increased severity and chronicity appear to increase risk. Risk to first-degree relatives: onset before 18 about 10-==35%==; the notes print 'onset after age 18: no increased risk to ~==15%=='. **MZ** twin concordance 53-==87%==; **DZ** 22-==47%==.
