blocks.note: **Q88**: a **SHANK3** mutation is associated with autism (explanation: **SHANK3** at 22q13.3; 22q13.3 deletion/Phelan-McDermid syndrome reduces cell-to-cell communication between neurons, with developmental delay, intellectual disability and absent or severely delayed speech; at least seven **SHANK3** mutations found in people with autism spectrum features). The notes' autism section lists chromosomes 2, 7 and 15 and fragile X but never mention **SHANK3**.

**Q2**: a mutation in **KISS1** is associated with Kallmann syndrome (explanation: kisspeptin and its receptor gate puberty onset; **KISS1** identified in X-linked or autosomal Kallmann syndrome, characterised by delayed or absent puberty and impaired sense of smell). Nothing on **KISS1** or Kallmann syndrome is in the notes.

blocks.subtopic: Argyll Robertson pupil and homonymous hemianopia
blocks.note: **Q85** (Argyll Robertson pupil: accommodation reflex present, light reflex absent; due to afferent defect in the pupillary pathway, probably pretectal) and **Q97** (right homonymous hemianopia from a left retrochiasmatic lesion such as optic radiation) appear in this question bank but are neurology/neuro-ophthalmology facts, not covered anywhere in the Molecular Genetics notes.

**Q42**: narcolepsy is associated with **HLA-DR2** (answer). The explanation contrasts cataplexy (narcolepsy: sudden loss of muscle tone) with catalepsy/waxy flexibility (catatonic features), and says loss of hypothalamic hypocretin-producing neurons causes it and that more than ==90%== of patients have the **HLA** **DQB1*0602** allele. Narcolepsy is not covered in the Molecular Genetics notes.

**Q25**: **HLA-DQB1*0602** is associated with narcolepsy (explanation: **HLA-DR2** haplotypes on chromosome 6; **HLA-DQB1*0602** and **DQA*0102** found in 85-==95%== of patients versus 12-==38%== of the general population). Not in the notes.

**Q48**: the gene that, when knocked out, gives mice resembling narcolepsy is orexin (explanation: hypocretin-1 and -2, also called orexin-A and -B, processed from preprohypocretin and made only in lateral hypothalamic cells). Not in the notes.

**Q44**: heritability of callous-unemotional traits is 30-==40%== (explanation: a meta-analysis of behaviour genetic studies in children with callous-unemotional traits and antisocial behaviour estimated ==41%== of variance genetic, ==16%== shared environment, ==43%== non-shared environment). The notes do not give this.

**Q50**: the specific phobia with a strongly genetic aetiology is blood injury injection phobia (explanation: its response to exposure is fainting with low blood pressure and bradycardia rather than tachycardia). The notes' specific-phobia figures (3-4 times in relatives) do not name it.

**Q53**: the gene most strongly implicated in **ADHD** is the dopamine 4 receptor gene (**DRD4**), whose brain mRNA distribution suggests a role in cognitive and executive functions. The notes' **ADHD** table gives risks and heritability but names no gene.

**Q97**: right homonymous hemianopia is caused by a lesion of the left optic radiation (explanation: left optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiations and striate cortex - any retrochiasmatic structure - can cause it). Neuro-ophthalmology, not in the Molecular Genetics notes.

items.text: Reduced 5-**HIAA** is found in high impulsive suicidality (decreased 5-**HIAA** is associated with suicidal, antisocial and violent behaviours; reduced serotonin may increase impulsivity).
Adopted child of alcohol-dependent parents: alcoholism risk about 4 times (adoptees' risk tracks the biological family, 1.6-3.6 times; close family members 4-fold).
Panic disorder in first-degree relatives: odds 4-8 times higher (relatives' prevalence 6-==17%==; up to 17 times if the index case's onset is below 20).

bullets.text: Autism: sibling recurrence 2-8% (RR 50); two affected siblings 25-30%; MZ concordance 60% (92% broad), DZ 0% (10% broad); ~90% heritability.
Fragile X: ~8% of autistic subjects have it; 16% of fragile X males are autistic; also tuberous sclerosis, NF, PKU.
ADHD: first-degree relatives 15-60% (RR 2-6); heritability ~70-80%; higher in male relatives.
Antisocial PD has the highest personality-disorder heritability (60-70%); most personality variation is non-shared environment.
Panic: OR 5 in first-degree relatives; ~17-fold if onset before 20 (6-fold after); heritability ~0.43.
Alcoholism: risk 4-6x in families; adoptees track biological parents (3-4x); GABRA2 (4p), ADH4, DRD2 A1.
Offspring risk: Tourette's 100-fold (25%), panic 12-fold (6%), anorexia 10-fold (5%), bipolar 8-9-fold (9%).
Autism heritability is about 90% (MZ concordance 60% classic, 92% broad vs DZ 0 and 10%).
Narcolepsy: HLA-DR2 association; cataplexy (not catalepsy/waxy flexibility), more than 90% carry HLA DQB1*0602.
Callous-unemotional traits: heritability 30-40% (meta-analysis 41% genetic, 16% shared, 43% non-shared environment).
ADHD: the gene most strongly implicated is the dopamine 4 receptor gene (DRD4).

blocks.text: Two approaches in a genetic clinic. Direct testing: like any other lab test, one individual is tested for a genotype already known to be associated with the illness. Gene tracking: many family members are tested to see whether the person seeking the test inherited the high-risk chromosome from a heterozygous parent; based on Mendelian principles (segregation of a chromosome within a family) and usable even when the exact locus is unknown.

blocks.title: Direct testing vs gene tracking
rows: The abnormality sought is already known to be associated with the illness
Not needed: usable even if the exact genetic locus is unknown
Like any other lab test (presence of a certain genotype)
Mendelian principles; segregation of a chromosome within a family

blocks.text: Prenatal identification: testing a fetus for a suspected genotype, usually prompted by family history or maternal factors (e.g. older mothers at risk of Down's). Maternal serum screening for neural tube defects and Down's is routinely offered in many countries. Adult-onset genetic conditions are not usually tested prenatally.

Genetic counselling is routinely offered with genetic tests: it gives information about risks and probabilities before the test and support (but not psychological) services afterwards. **NHS** Regional Genetic Centres combine cytogenetic, molecular and clinical genetic services and offer familial (carrier) testing, diagnostic and prenatal (presymptomatic) testing.
**DNA** banks provide secure, long-term storage of an individual's genetic material; beneficial for biomedical research but possible misuse raises ethical issues.

bullets.text: Direct testing: one person, known association; gene tracking: many family members, works without a known locus.
Prenatal testing is based on family history or maternal factors; adult-onset conditions are not usually tested prenatally.
Genetic counselling gives risk information before testing and support (not psychological) afterwards.
NHS Regional Genetic Centres combine cytogenetic, molecular and clinical genetics services.
DNA banks store genetic material long term; research benefit but ethical concerns about misuse.

children.label: Four phases: G1, S, G2, M (G1/G2 = growth phases, S = synthetic phase, M = mitosis).
Growth factors (EGF, PDGF, IGF) push quiescent G0 cells into the cycle via transcription factors and DNA synthesis.
S phase: the 46 chromosomes are duplicated into chromatids.
Liver cells can pause temporarily in G0; neurons stay in G0 indefinitely.
Interphase (G0, G1, S, G2) is the longest 'holding' phase in which DNA and organelles are replicated.
Mitosis: prophase, metaphase (equatorial alignment), anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase (cytokinesis starts).
Meiosis gives 4 daughter cells with half the chromosome number; mitosis gives 2 with the same number.
Meiosis I is the reduction division with synapsis (crossing over); meiosis II is like normal mitosis.
Humans are diploid: 46 chromosomes = 22 autosome pairs + XY/XX; gametes are haploid.
Only trisomies 13, 18 and 21 survive to birth; triploidy/tetraploidy cause spontaneous abortion.
Down's: trisomy 21, 1:700; 95% meiotic non-disjunction (age-related), 4% Robertsonian translocation, 1% mosaicism.
Edwards' = trisomy 18 (1:8000, rocker-bottom feet); Patau's = trisomy 13 (1:6000, polydactyly, cleft lip/palate).
Turner's (45X): about 1 in 2000 live-born females; in 80% the missing chromosome is paternal so the single X is maternal.
Mosaics (post-fertilisation mitotic non-disjunction) have milder malformations.
Chimerism = 2+ cell lines from different zygotes; mosaicism = distinct lineages from the same zygote.
Polyploidy = extra sets of chromosomes (triploidy 3n, tetraploidy 4n).
Nucleoside = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar; nucleotide = phosphorylated nucleoside.
Purines A, G; pyrimidines T, C; only TA, AT, GC, CG pairs; RNA single-stranded in humans.
Codon = three nucleotides coding one amino acid; 20 amino acids but 64 codons (degenerate code).
Exons code; introns are non-coding and removed from mRNA before it leaves the nucleus.

mindMap.label: 5. Synthesis of DNA, RNA and protein

children.label: Replication = DNA from DNA; transcription (nucleus) = RNA from DNA; translation (cytoplasm, ribosomes) = protein from RNA.
hnRNA is spliced (introns removed) to make mRNA; tRNAs are made separately in the nucleus.
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (Mg2+, energy-dependent) activates amino acids; one enzyme per amino acid.
Translation: initiation, elongation, termination; methionine-tRNA binds the P site; stops UAA, UGA, UAG.
Posttranslational modification occurs in ER and Golgi; faulty proteins are tagged for lysosomal destruction.
Microsatellite tandem repeats underlie the trinucleotide repeat disorders.
Point mutations: transition (purine-purine / pyrimidine-pyrimidine, A to G) vs transversion (purine-pyrimidine, A to T).
Frame shift = not multiples of three; in-frame = multiples of three; silent/mis-sense/non-sense describe protein effect.
Robertsonian translocation: two acrocentric chromosomes fuse, p arms lost; balanced carrier but risk of monosomy/trisomy gametes (Down's).
DiGeorge 22q11.2: AD, hypocalcemia from absent/malformed parathyroids, >25% psychosis; 25% schizophrenia risk if offspring has deletion.
Williams 7q11: hypercalcemia at birth, supravalvular aortic stenosis, fluent-seeming speech, hyperacusis.
Angelman = maternal 15q11-13 deletion; Prader-Willi = paternal 15q11-13 deletion; Cri-du-chat = 5p deletion; Smith Magenis = 17p11.2.
Law of uniformity: DD x dd gives all Dd (intermediate phenotypes from co-dominance show it is not entirely true).
Law of segregation: one allele per parent passed on by chance; Dd x Dd = 1 DD : 2 Dd : 1 dd.
Law of independent assortment: allele pairs pass on independently; DdHh x ddhh gives four equally likely types.
Mendelian traits are categorical (all or none); not applicable in the same simple way to IQ or blood pressure.
AD: 50% risk from one heterozygous parent, 75% if both heterozygous; incomplete penetrance and variable expression; phenocopy.
AR: two carriers give 1 in 4 affected, 1 in 2 carriers, 1 in 4 normal; consanguinity raises risk; enzymatic proteins.
X inactivation is random, early, irreversible, via DNA methylation; Barr body; trisomy X = two Barr bodies.
X-linked recessive: no male-to-male transmission; unfavourable Lyonisation makes manifesting heterozygote females.
X-linked dominant: rare; Rett syndrome and vitamin D-resistant rickets; affected father gives all daughters, no sons.
Lesch-Nyhan: Xq26-27, XLR, HGPRT deficiency, self-mutilation (lip/finger biting), hyperuricemia.
XLMR: syndromic 1/3, non-syndromic 2/3; Fragile X most common; MECP2 gives Rett.
Both parents affected by an AR disorder: all children affected (100%); two carriers: 1 in 4.
Tay-Sachs: hexosaminidase A deficiency, autosomal recessive.
Mitochondrial DNA is purely maternal (no sperm mitochondria); no introns so mutations bite; MELAS, LHON, CPEO, MERRF, Kearns-Sayre type disorders.
Trinucleotide repeats: Fragile X CGG, Friedreich GAA, Huntington CAG, myotonic dystrophy CTG; anticipation = earlier/worse with each generation.
Fragile X: 1 in 4000, CGG beyond 52 destabilises, 200+ repeats lower IQ; premutation carriers get tremor/ataxia (women: ovarian failure).
Huntington's: AD, full penetrance, CAG on 4p16.3, 40-55 repeats adult onset (30-50 y), >70 juvenile; paternal expansion.
Myotonic dystrophy and Fragile X: anticipation higher maternally (oogenesis); Huntington's higher paternally.
Imprinting: paternal 15q11-q13 deletion = Prader-Willi (~70%, maternal UPD ~25%); maternal deletion = Angelman (paternal UPD ~4%).
Multifactorial = genes + environment (liability/threshold); polygenic = additive genes, no environment.
Polymorphism = variant in at least 1% of the population with normal (non-disease) phenotype; ABO blood groups.
RFLP (Southern blotting), SNPs (sequencing/DNA chips), VNTRs: microsatellites 2-6 bases (preferred, PCR), minisatellites 20-70 bases.
Maintained by founder effect, genetic drift, natural selection; mostly in non-coding regions.
5HTTLPR is in the promoter; short allele = low transporter expression; 55% of Europeans have the long allele.
Caspi 2003: short-allele carriers show more depression/suicidality after stressful life events (gene-environment interaction).
Southern = DNA, Western = protein, Northern = RNA.
PCR: primers needed, so target sequence must be known; amplifies over a million-fold from tiny samples; contaminants can be amplified.
PCR has three steps: heat denaturation, cooling/annealing with primers, polymerase extension; cycles double the copies.
FISH uses fluorescent probes to localise specific DNA sequences on chromosomes.
DNA cloning inserts a fragment into a vector (plasmid, bacteriophage or virus) using DNA ligase to make clones.
Thymidine-deprived cell culture makes fragile sites visible for diagnosing fragile X.
Huntington's disease is diagnosed by PCR repeat counting (more than 35 repeats in adults, more than 50 in children); karyotype shows only macroscopic defects.
Concordance: MZ > DZ implies a genetic component; equal MZ and DZ concordance implies none.
Heritability = proportion of trait variance that is genetic; narrow-sense (additive) vs broad-sense (additive + non-additive).
High heritability does NOT mean genetic determination or genes of large effect; Mendelian single-gene disorders = 100%.
Heritability estimates: schizophrenia 80, bipolar >80, major depression 40, GAD 30, panic 40, phobia 35, alcohol dependence 60.
Autism and Tourette's may be about 90% heritable; IQ 0.5-0.8; Big Five 42-57%.

mindMap.label: 11. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, epistasis, heterogeneity and pleiotropy

children.label: Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1; p squared normal homozygote, q squared affected, 2pq carriers.
Notes' example: incidence 1 in 3600 gives q = 1/60 and carriers 2pq = 1/30.
HWE fails with selection, genetic drift (founder effect), gene flow, consanguinity, and high mutation rates.
Locus heterogeneity = same phenotype, different loci (early onset AD: chromosomes 1, 14, 21).
Allelic heterogeneity = same locus, different mutations (cystic fibrosis, ~600 mutations on chromosome 7).
Pleiotropy = one mutation, many organ systems (Marfan's); epistasis = gene-gene interaction.
Two affected AR parents with a normal child = locus heterogeneity (different loci in each parent).

mindMap.label: 12. Types of genetic studies; classical genetic studies

children.label: Four paradigms: basic genetic epidemiology, advanced genetic epidemiology, gene finding, molecular genetics.
MZ twins share 100% of genes (70% share a chorion); DZ twins share 50%, like siblings.
Probandwise concordance = affected twins / total co-twins; pairwise = concordant pairs / total pairs.
MZ/DZ concordance: male alcoholism 41/22, female alcoholism 34/31, panic 24/11, bulimia 23/9, ADHD 58/31, autism 64/9, Tourette's 53/8.
Family history method: practical but many false negatives; family study: few false results but expensive.
Relative risks: ADHD 55x, autism 45x, schizophrenia 10x, bipolar 7-11x, alcoholism 4-6x, panic 3-8x.
Adoption studies: parent-as-proband, adoptee-as-proband, cross-fostering; problems: adoption itself is a risk and matching of families.
Linkage: closer loci recombine less; recombination frequency gives distance; 1 cM = 1% recombination = ~1 Mb.
LOD >3 = linkage (1,000:1); LOD <= -2 = non-linkage (100:1).
Sib pairs share 0/1/2 alleles with probability 0.25/0.5/0.25; small-effect loci need 600-800 pairs.
Whole genome scan: e.g. 950 microsatellites in 110 Icelanders found neuregulin-1 for schizophrenia.
Association studies: case-control, candidate genes, TDT; GWAS = thousands of SNPs in thousands of people.
Linkage: families, >10 cM, large effects (RR >2); association: cases/controls, <1 cM, small effects (OR <2).

mindMap.label: 12C. Alternative approaches: transgenics, epigenetics, position effects, endophenotypes

children.label: Transgenics: insert a modified (mouse) gene to study function directly.
Epigenetics: DNA methylation + histone modification explain most epigenetic variation; Crow links it to schizophrenia concordance.
Position effects: gene activity depends on chromosomal neighbourhood, altered by translocation.
Endophenotype (Gottesman and Shields, 1975): measurable marker between genotype and disease with six criteria incl. heritable, state-independent, higher in relatives.
Schizophrenia endophenotypes: working memory, prepulse inhibition, smooth pursuit, glial cell changes.
Clinical symptom clusters such as negative symptoms do not fit the endophenotype criteria.

mindMap.label: 13A. Psychiatric genetics: causal models and practical difficulties

children.label: Mendelian families and single genes of major effect are not found; association odds ratios 1-2 (median 1.3).
Risk falls rapidly and non-linearly from MZ co-twin (50-60%) to first-degree relatives (~10%): many interacting modest-effect factors.
Difficulties: ethnic variation, ascertainment, arbitrary DSM/ICD phenotypes.
Common disease-common variant model (many small-effect polymorphisms) is currently more popular than rare-variant model.
Psychiatric disorders: vague boundaries, multiple phenocopies, incomplete penetrance, non-linear risk, MZ concordance 30-70%.
Candidate genes: NRG1 8p12-p21, DTNBP1 6p22, G72 13q34, DAAO 12q24, RGS4 1q21-22, COMT 22q11, DISC1 1q42.
One parent affected: 13% risk to child; both parents: 46%; half sibling 4%; children/siblings about 10-fold.
MZ concordance 41-65%, DZ 0-28%, broad heritability 80%.
Schizotypal PD is the commonest personality disorder in relatives (nearly 15%).
Earlier onset (before age 21) means higher familial risk; symptom dimensions show only weak familial aggregation.
Down's syndrome: schizophrenia risk the same as or lower than the general population (<0.6%).
Question key: MZ schizophrenia concordance 44-50% (0.48), DZ 10-15%, about three times higher in MZ.
One parent with mood disorder: child risk 10-25%; both parents: roughly doubles.
Bipolar proband: first-degree relatives bipolar 5-10% (RR 8), unipolar 10-20% (RR 2-3); MZ co-twin bipolar 40-70% (RR 60).
Bipolar genes: BDNF 11p13, DAO G72/G30 13q33, COMT 22q11, BCR; X-linked Xq24-q27.1 in a Finnish pedigree.
MDD: first-degree relatives 5-30% (RR 1.1-4.0); MZ 40%, DZ 11%; heritability meta-analysis 31-42%.
Earlier onset (<25-30) and recurrence raise risk to relatives of MDD probands.
Schizoaffective: highest risk to relatives for any psychiatric disorder; manic type gives more bipolar, depressive type more schizophrenia.
5HTT, MAOA, COMT each add 10-20% bipolar risk and show gene-environment effects; GRK3 identified via an animal model.
Question key: 15-20% prevalence in first-degree relatives of bipolar patients (MZ concordance up to 79%, DZ 19%).
A twin brother of an affected woman is dizygotic: bipolar risk 5-15%.
Both MAO-A and MAO-B are encoded on chromosome X.
Familial early-onset AD: APP (chr 21), presenilin 1 (chr 14), presenilin 2 (chr 1); up to 50% of familial presenile AD but <1% of all patients.
APOE (19q): highest attributable risk; 4/4 OR 14.9, 3/4 OR 3.2; onset two decades earlier in 4 homozygotes.
ApoE absolute risk: 4 homozygote 35% male / 53% female; 4 heterozygote 12% / 23%; no 4: 4.6% / 9.3%.
First-degree relatives of AD probands: 15-19% vs 5% in controls (3-4x); MZ 84% vs DZ 40% probandwise concordance.
CADASIL: NOTCH3 on 19p13.1-13.2; mutations mostly exon 4.
FTLD: MAPT (tau) and progranulin (PGRN) both on 17q21.
Lewy body dementia: no specific gene; Parkinson's loci PARK1/4 (alpha-synuclein 4q21), PARK2 (Parkin 6q25), PARK8 (LRRK2), PARK6 (PINK1), PARK7 (DJ-1).
Autism: sibling recurrence 2-8% (RR 50); two affected siblings 25-30%; MZ concordance 60% (92% broad), DZ 0% (10% broad); ~90% heritability.
Fragile X: ~8% of autistic subjects have it; 16% of fragile X males are autistic; also tuberous sclerosis, NF, PKU.
ADHD: first-degree relatives 15-60% (RR 2-6); heritability ~70-80%; higher in male relatives.
Antisocial PD has the highest personality-disorder heritability (60-70%); most personality variation is non-shared environment.
Panic: OR 5 in first-degree relatives; ~17-fold if onset before 20 (6-fold after); heritability ~0.43.
Alcoholism: risk 4-6x in families; adoptees track biological parents (3-4x); GABRA2 (4p), ADH4, DRD2 A1.
Offspring risk: Tourette's 100-fold (25%), panic 12-fold (6%), anorexia 10-fold (5%), bipolar 8-9-fold (9%).
Autism heritability is about 90% (MZ concordance 60% classic, 92% broad vs DZ 0 and 10%).
Narcolepsy: HLA-DR2 association; cataplexy (not catalepsy/waxy flexibility), more than 90% carry HLA DQB1*0602.
Callous-unemotional traits: heritability 30-40% (meta-analysis 41% genetic, 16% shared, 43% non-shared environment).
ADHD: the gene most strongly implicated is the dopamine 4 receptor gene (DRD4).
Direct testing: one person, known association; gene tracking: many family members, works without a known locus.
Prenatal testing is based on family history or maternal factors; adult-onset conditions are not usually tested prenatally.
Genetic counselling gives risk information before testing and support (not psychological) afterwards.
NHS Regional Genetic Centres combine cytogenetic, molecular and clinical genetics services.
DNA banks store genetic material long term; research benefit but ethical concerns about misuse.
